d: Two ways to write a graph down. The matrix suits the algebra behind every spectral ranking; compressed lists are how a real web graph fits in memory.
a: Adjacency matrix Adjacency list CSR Compressed sparse row
x: A graph needs a concrete representation before a program can rank it. The adjacency matrix writes it as a table of zeros and ones, which makes linear algebra available: PageRank , Eigenvector centrality , Katz centrality and hits are all statements about this matrix. The adjacency list stores, for each node, only the nodes it links to, which is the only form that fits a web graph in memory. Every serious implementation thinks in matrices and computes with lists. The adjacency matrix Number the nodes to . The adjacency matrix is the matrix with Row lists ’s out-links and column lists ’s in-links. For the running example, with rows and columns in the order A to G: The last two rows are empty because F and G link nowhere; the fifth column is empty because nothing links to E. What the algebra buys Matrix products answer graph questions directly: Degrees. With the all-ones vector, gives every out-degree and every in-degree (see Degree ). Walks. counts the walks of exactly steps from to . In the example, : E reaches A through D and through C. Katz centrality sums these counts over all with decaying weights. Transition probabilities. Divide each non-empty row by its sum to get the matrix with for each link. Row of is the probability distribution of a random walk that leaves along a random out-link. PageRank is the long-run distribution of a walk on a repaired version of . Spectral rankings. Eigenvector centrality is the dominant eigenvector of , and hits uses the dominant eigenvectors of and . Why nobody stores the matrix A dense matrix needs entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph, , so even one bit per entry takes bits, about 1.8 petabytes. Yet only 2,450,405,793 entries are ones: 0.000017% of the matrix. Web graphs are extremely sparse , with an average of 20 links per node however large grows. Storage must scale with the number of arcs , not with . Adjacency lists and CSR An adjacency list stores each node’s out-neighbours. The compact way to do this is compressed sparse row (CSR): one array holding every node’s successors back to back, sorted by source, and an offsets array marking where each node’s run begins. For the running example (A = 0, …, G = 6): offsets: 0 2 3 5 7 10 10 10 node u's successors are targets[offsets[u] .. offsets[u+1]) targets: 1 2 | 2 | 0 6 | 0 2 | 2 3 5 Node E (index 4) owns targets[7..10) = 2, 3, 5, that is C, D and F. F and G own empty runs, so their offsets repeat. The costs are easy to state: Structure Size At Common Crawl’s scale Offsets, 32-bit bytes 479 MB Targets, 32-bit bytes 9.8 GB Same again for in-links (the transpose) 10.3 GB The offsets fit in 32 bits only because 2.45 billion arcs is below ; a page-level graph with tens of billions of arcs needs 64-bit offsets. CSR makes the inner loop of PageRank a straight scan. A “pull” iteration walks each node’s in-links in the transposed graph and sums contributions, reading the targets array once from start to end. Sequential reads of the arc array cost little; the random reads of score vectors cost the most (see pagerank-at-scale). Compressed lists Sorted successor lists have structure that CSR ignores. Neighbouring nodes in a well-chosen order link to similar targets, and consecutive targets differ by small gaps. The WebGraph framework exploits both and stores Common Crawl’s domain graph in 15.1 bits per arc, 4.6 GB instead of 9.8 GB for the targets alone, while still decoding a node’s successors quickly. How well this works depends on the order of the nodes; see node-orderings. The transpose Many measures look at in-links: Harmonic centrality needs distances to a node, and pull-style PageRank sums over in-links. Both use the transposed graph , which reverses every arc. Common Crawl ships its graph in both directions for this reason: domain.graph holds out-links and domain-t.graph holds in-links, 4.6 GB each. References Saad, Y. (2003). Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems (2nd ed.). SIAM, section 3.4 on sparse storage formats. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602.

d: A node is central if many shortest paths between other nodes pass through it. Betweenness finds bridges and brokers, not popular destinations.
a: Betweenness Freeman betweenness Brokerage
x: Betweenness centrality scores a node by how often it lies on the shortest paths between other nodes. Linton Freeman defined it in 1977 to capture brokerage: the person through whom information between two groups must pass holds power even if few people know them directly. On a link graph, a high-betweenness node is a bridge that connects regions which would otherwise be far apart. It answers a different question from PageRank or Harmonic centrality , which score destinations. Definition Let be the number of shortest paths from to , and the number of those that pass through . The betweenness of is summed over ordered pairs with reachable from . When several shortest paths tie, each gets an equal share of the credit. On a directed graph, dividing by scales the result to . Worked example On the running example only three nodes lie inside any shortest path: Node C A D B, E, F, G Betweenness 6 3 1 0 C earns 6. It is the only route for A → G, B → A, B → G, D → G and E → G, which gives 5, and it lies on one of the two shortest paths for E → A (E → C → A and E → D → A) and for E → B (E → C → A → B and E → D → A → B), which gives two halves. A earns 3: C → B, D → B and E → B all pass through it. D earns 1 from the other halves of E → A and E → B. E, the hub with three out-links, scores 0: shortest paths start at E but never pass through it, because nothing links to E. What betweenness captures Bridges and bottlenecks. A node joining two otherwise separate communities collects every path between them. Removing it lengthens or breaks those paths. Betweenness is the standard tool for finding single points of failure in networks. Brokers, not stars. A node can have small in-degree and huge betweenness, and a popular node deep inside one community can have little. In the running example, G has in-degree 1 and harmonic centrality 3 but zero betweenness, because no shortest path continues past it. Community structure. The Girvan–Newman algorithm removes the arcs with the highest betweenness, the arcs between communities, one at a time until the graph falls apart into groups (see community-detection). Axioms In Boldi and Vigna’s tests betweenness satisfies only the half of the size axiom: in a graph made of a clique and a separate long cycle, cycle nodes carry many paths while clique nodes carry none, because every pair of clique nodes is directly linked. It fails density and score monotonicity: a new link to can create shortcuts that bypass and lower its score (see Axioms for centrality ). These are not defects so much as a reminder that betweenness measures brokerage, not prominence. Computing it The naive method counts shortest paths for every pair, or worse. Brandes’ algorithm (2001) computes exact betweenness for all nodes in time on unweighted graphs: one breadth-first search per source, followed by a backward sweep that accumulates each node’s share. That is the algorithm behind every serious implementation, and behind the numbers above. is still out of reach on a web graph. For Common Crawl’s domain graph it means about arc visits. Large-scale betweenness is therefore estimated by sampling: Source sampling (Brandes and Pich, 2007) runs the BFS from a random sample of sources and scales up. A few thousand sources rank the top nodes well. Path sampling (Riondato and Kornaropoulos, 2014) samples random shortest paths and uses VC-dimension bounds to fix the sample size needed for a given additive error, independent of the graph’s size. Neither Common Crawl nor the commercial link indexes publish betweenness for domains. Betweenness on the web On a domain graph, nodes with high betweenness are the connectors between linguistic, national and topical regions: large portals, reference sites, platforms hosting content from many communities, and infrastructure domains that appear in pages everywhere. Betweenness explains network resilience better than it explains importance. A domain can be a crucial bridge and still attract little traffic or trust. For a domain buyer, betweenness rarely matters directly. It becomes useful when mapping a suspected link-spam network: computed on the network’s own subgraph, it shows which few domains hold the network together. Variants Edge betweenness counts shortest paths through each arc instead of each node. It drives Girvan–Newman community detection. Load and flow betweenness spread credit along all paths or along network flows rather than only along shortest paths. Random-walk betweenness (Newman, 2005) counts how often a random walk from to passes through , which suits networks where things do not travel along shortest paths. References Freeman, L. C. (1977). A set of measures of centrality based on betweenness. Sociometry 40(1), 35–41. Brandes, U. (2001). A faster algorithm for betweenness centrality. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 25(2), 163–177. Brandes, U., & Pich, C. (2007). Centrality estimation in large networks. International Journal of Bifurcation and Chaos 17(7), 2303–2318. Riondato, M., & Kornaropoulos, E. M. (2014). Fast approximation of betweenness centrality through sampling. WSDM 2014 , 413–422.

d: Seen from its largest strongly connected component, the web looks like a bow tie. Pages that reach the core sit on one side, pages the core reaches sit on the other, and stragglers hang off both.
a: Bow tie Bowtie model IN component OUT component Tendrils
x: In 1999 a team from AltaVista, IBM and Compaq mapped a crawl of 203 million pages and found that its connectivity had a shape. A giant core of pages all reach each other. An IN set of pages reach the core but cannot be reached from it, and an OUT set can be reached from the core but cannot get back. Drawn with IN on the left and OUT on the right, the picture looks like a bow tie. The model gives names to the parts of any directed graph relative to its largest strongly connected component , and those parts behave very differently under every ranking method. CORE largest SCC IN reaches the core OUT reached from it tube: IN to OUT, bypassing the core tendril tendril disconnected The bow-tie decomposition. Every node belongs to exactly one part, defined by whether it can reach the core, can be reached from it, both, or neither. The parts Let be the largest strongly connected component. Every other node falls into one part: CORE: the nodes of . Every core node reaches every other. IN: nodes that reach but cannot be reached from it. New sites that link to popular sites before anyone links back live here. OUT: nodes reachable from that cannot reach it. Corporate sites that link only internally, and pages the crawler found but did not fetch, live here. TENDRILS: nodes reachable from IN that cannot reach the core, and nodes that reach OUT without being reachable from the core. TUBES: paths from IN to OUT that bypass the core. DISCONNECTED: nodes with no path to or from the core in either direction. In the running example (see The web graph ) the core is {A, B, C}. D and E form IN, since both reach the core and nothing in the core reaches them. G is OUT. F is a tendril: E, in IN, reaches it, but F cannot reach the core. Computing the decomposition The decomposition costs a few linear passes: Find the strongly connected components and pick the largest, (Tarjan’s algorithm, one depth-first search). Run a breadth-first search forward from all of at once. Every node it reaches outside belongs to OUT or to the parts hanging off it. Run a breadth-first search backward, on the transposed graph, from . Every node it reaches outside belongs to IN. Search forward from IN and backward from OUT, skipping the core, to separate tendrils and tubes from the disconnected remainder. Each search costs , so the whole decomposition is linear in the size of the graph (see Paths, distance and reachability ). How big are the parts? The proportions depend heavily on the crawl: Part Broder et al., 1999 crawl Meusel et al., Common Crawl 2012 Pages 203 million 3.5 billion CORE 27.7% 51.3% IN 21.3% 32.0% OUT 21.2% 6.1% Everything else (tendrils, tubes, disconnected) 29.7% 10.7% Broder’s crawl gave four parts of nearly equal size, a striking symmetry that became textbook material. Thirteen years later, Meusel, Vigna, Lehmberg and Bizer found a core twice as large and a tiny OUT set in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. They argued that the proportions depend largely on how a crawl is gathered, so they describe the crawler as much as the web. The shape recurs; the sizes do not. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has a core of 30,219,288 domains, 25.2% of the total. Its 76 million domains with no recorded out-links cannot be in the core or in IN, so they must sit in OUT, the tendrils or the disconnected remainder. Most of them are domains the crawl saw only as link targets. Why the parts matter for ranking Random surfers drain into OUT. A random walk can leave the core for OUT but never return. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would end up in OUT and in other sinks. The damping-factor and the treatment of dangling-nodes exist largely because of this part of the bow tie. IN pages have no in-link credit from the core. Under Eigenvector centrality , IN nodes score exactly zero, since no walk from the core reaches them. Harmonic centrality gives them small but nonzero scores, from whatever IN nodes link to them. Core membership is a quality signal. A site that the core links to and that links back into it is embedded in the web’s mainstream. Spam networks often sit outside the core: they link to popular sites, or to each other and their targets, but the core rarely links back. trustrank exploits the same asymmetry by spreading trust outward from hand-checked sites, which seldom link to spam. The fractal view Each part of the bow tie, examined alone, often looks like a smaller bow tie. Dill and colleagues found the pattern in thematically and geographically defined subsets of the web as early as 2002. The bow tie is less a fixed architecture than the generic shape of a directed graph built by many independent actors who link mostly to things that already exist. References Broder, A., Kumar, R., Maghoul, F., Raghavan, P., Rajagopalan, S., Stata, R., Tomkins, A., & Wiener, J. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited: a trick of the heavy tail. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432. Dill, S., Kumar, R., McCurley, K. S., Rajagopalan, S., Sivakumar, D., & Tomkins, A. (2002). Self-similarity in the web. ACM Transactions on Internet Technology 2(3), 205–223.

d: Boldi and Vigna's three tests (size, density and score monotonicity) check whether a centrality measure agrees with intuition on graphs simple enough that the right answer is obvious. Only harmonic centrality passes all three.
a: Size axiom Density axiom Score monotonicity Boldi–Vigna axioms
x: With dozens of centrality measures in use, how do you pick one? In 2014 Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna proposed to test measures against small graphs where everyone agrees on the right answer, the way physical theories are tested against simple experiments. They defined three axioms , checked eleven classical measures against them, and found that only one, Harmonic centrality , satisfies all three. Common Crawl, which had Vigna’s help building its graph tooling, has ranked hosts by harmonic centrality since 2017. The size axiom Consider the graph : a -clique (every pair of the nodes linked both ways) next to a directed cycle of nodes, with no arcs between the two. Which nodes should be more central? Intuition says size should win. If the cycle is long enough, its nodes should beat the clique’s, because they belong to a larger community; if the clique is large enough, its nodes should win instead. Formally, a measure satisfies the size axiom if: for every there is a such that for all , cycle nodes score strictly higher than clique nodes; and for every there is a such that for all , clique nodes score strictly higher than cycle nodes. A measure that satisfies only the second half is marked “only ” below, and one that satisfies only the first, “only ”. Harmonic centrality passes. A clique node is at distance 1 from the other clique nodes, so it scores . A cycle node is at distances from the others along the cycle, so it scores , the harmonic number, which grows like without bound. Each side wins once it is large enough. Closeness fails: a clique node’s closeness is and a cycle node’s is , so growing the clique lowers its score. PageRank fails both halves: every node of gets exactly , whatever the sizes. The density axiom Now join a -clique and a -cycle by a single bidirectional arc between a clique node and a cycle node . Call the graph . When both sides have the same number of nodes, but the clique has far more arcs. A measure satisfies the density axiom if, for , scores strictly higher than : being embedded in a denser neighbourhood should help. Most spectral measures pass this test, since the dominant eigenvector concentrates where arcs are dense. Closeness, Lin’s index and betweenness fail it. Betweenness fails because also carries the cycle’s own traffic: in a directed cycle, every path between two other nodes that wraps past runs through it, while the clique’s nodes are all adjacent and carry none of each other’s paths. Score monotonicity The third axiom is about change. A measure satisfies score monotonicity if, for every graph and every pair of nodes and with no arc from to , adding the arc strictly increases ’s score. Receiving a new link should always help. It sounds trivial, yet several famous measures fail it. Adding an arc never lengthens a distance, yet it can lower ’s closeness: nodes that could not reach before now can, and each adds a term to ’s sum of distances. Eigenvector centrality and HITS can shift their dominant eigenvector away from ’s part of the graph. The results Boldi and Vigna’s table: Measure Size Density Score monotonicity Degree only yes yes Harmonic yes yes yes Closeness no no no Lin’s index only no no Betweenness only no no Dominant eigenvector only yes no Seeley’s index no yes no Katz only yes yes PageRank no yes yes HITS only yes no SALSA no yes no Degree satisfies only the half of the size axiom because cycle nodes always have in-degree 1, however long the cycle. Betweenness satisfies only the half because clique nodes lie on no shortest paths between other nodes, so they score zero, while a long cycle routes many paths through each of its nodes. What the axioms do and do not say The axioms are tests, not a definition. A measure that fails one is not useless; it formalises a different notion of importance. Betweenness is the right tool for finding bridges and bottlenecks precisely because it ignores density. The tests do expose behaviour that matters on the web: Closeness fails everything because of how it treats unreachable nodes. On a web graph, where most pairs cannot reach each other, that is fatal (see Closeness centrality ). PageRank fails size because it normalises scores to a probability distribution and spreads teleportation evenly. A large community and a small one of the same shape get the same per-node scores. Harmonic centrality passes all three , at the cost of being expensive to compute exactly: it needs the distances from every node. The hyperball algorithm makes approximate harmonic centrality affordable on graphs with billions of arcs. Later work by Boldi, Luongo and Vigna added rank monotonicity , which asks that a new link to never let a node that was below overtake it. That axiom, too, separates measures that look alike on paper. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Boldi, P., Luongo, A., & Vigna, S. (2017). Rank monotonicity in centrality measures. Network Science 5(4), 529–550. Sabidussi, G. (1966). The centrality index of a graph. Psychometrika 31(4), 581–603.

d: A centrality measure assigns every node a score of importance computed from the graph's structure alone. Different measures formalise different ideas of importance, and they disagree.
a: Centrality measure Node importance Link analysis
x: A centrality is a function that assigns every node of a graph a number, computed from the arcs alone, meant to say how important the node is. “Important” has no single meaning, so there is no single centrality. A node can matter because many nodes link to it, because it is close to everything, because shortest paths pass through it, or because important nodes link to it. Each idea leads to a family of measures, and on the same graph they produce different rankings. Three families Boldi and Vigna sort the classical measures into three families: Geometric measures score a node by its distances from the other nodes. In-degree counts the nodes at distance 1; Closeness centrality , Harmonic centrality and Lin’s index aggregate all distances. Path-based measures count paths through or into a node. Betweenness centrality counts the shortest paths passing through a node; Katz centrality counts all walks ending at it, weighting long walks less. Spectral measures take the dominant eigenvector of a matrix derived from the graph. Eigenvector centrality , PageRank , hits and salsa belong here, and so does Katz, viewed differently. Spectral measures embody the recursive idea, important nodes are those that important nodes link to, which is why they dominate web search. Geometric measures are easier to explain and, as the Axioms for centrality entry shows, often behave better. One graph, many rankings Here is every measure on the running example (see The web graph ), with nodes ordered from highest to lowest score. Ties share a position. Measure Ranking (highest first) Top score In-degree C · A · B = D = F = G · E 4 Harmonic C · A = G · B · D = F · E 4 Closeness D = F · C · A · B · G · E 1 Betweenness C · A · D · B = E = F = G 6 Eigenvector C · A = G · B · D = E = F 0.325 Katz () C · A · G · B · D = F · E 1.868 PageRank () C · A · G · B · D = F · E 0.298 HITS authority C · A · D = F · B · G · E 0.438 HITS hub E · D · A · B · C · F = G 0.289 Most measures agree that C is the most important node; it receives four of the ten links and sits in the middle of the core. Below C they diverge: Closeness puts D and F first. Each is reached only from E, at distance 1, so the average distance to them is 1, the best possible. The measure rewards having few, close in-neighbours, an artefact the Closeness centrality entry explains. Eigenvector centrality gives D, E and F exactly zero. The core cannot reach them, and the dominant eigenvector lives on the core and what it feeds (see Strongly connected components ). G outranks B under harmonic, Katz, eigenvector and PageRank, though both have one in-link. G’s in-link comes from C, the most central node, and B’s from A. HITS hubs reverse the picture. E links to three nodes that are good authorities, so it is the best hub, though nothing links to it. You can change the graph and compare the measures yourself: Incoming or outgoing? On a directed graph every measure comes in two versions: one built from in-links and one from out-links. For importance on the web the incoming version is the meaningful one, because what links to a site is controlled by others, while what a site links to is controlled by its owner (see The web graph ). All the measures in this encyclopedia use incoming links unless they say otherwise. The outgoing versions have uses too: HITS hubs score good link lists, and cheirank is PageRank on the reversed graph. Choosing a measure Four questions narrow the choice: What does importance mean here? Attention (PageRank), reachability (harmonic), brokerage (betweenness) and endorsement by the right sources (trustrank, Personalized PageRank ) are different questions. Does the measure behave sensibly? The Axioms for centrality entry tests measures against simple graphs where the right answer is obvious. Harmonic centrality passes all three tests; closeness fails all three. Can you afford it? Degree costs one pass over the arcs and PageRank a few dozen. Exact betweenness and closeness need a search from every node, which is impossible on a billion-arc graph without approximation (see hyperball and brandes-algorithm). Can it be gamed? Any measure that rewards incoming links can be inflated by manufacturing them. Measures differ in how much a spammer gains per fake link (see link-spam and spam-mass). Centrality on the real web Common Crawl publishes two centralities for every host and domain: Harmonic centrality and PageRank . On its 2026 domain graph they agree at the top: the same infrastructure domains ( googleapis.com , google.com , facebook.com ) lead both. Their Spearman correlation over the 119,453 auction domains present in the graph on 2026-09-23 is 0.69 (see spearman-rho). Large disagreements further down reveal what each measure rewards, as the PageRank entry shows with domains that rank in PageRank’s top 30 but outside harmonic centrality’s top 900. References Freeman, L. C. (1978). Centrality in social networks: conceptual clarification. Social Networks 1(3), 215–239. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Newman, M. E. J. (2018). Networks (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press, chapter 7.

d: A node is central if it is close, on average, to all other nodes. A classic idea from social network analysis that breaks down on graphs where most pairs cannot reach each other, like the web.
a: Closeness Bavelas closeness Lin's index Lin centrality
x: Closeness centrality scores a node by how near the rest of the graph is. Alex Bavelas proposed it in 1950 for small communication networks, where the person who can reach everyone in the fewest steps is best placed to coordinate. The idea is appealing and the formula is simple: one over the sum of distances. On graphs that are not strongly connected, which includes every web graph, the formula needs patching, and the patches produce rankings that defy common sense. Harmonic centrality fixes the problem, which is why it has largely replaced closeness in link analysis. Definition On a strongly connected graph, the closeness of is the reciprocal of the sum of distances to it: Some authors multiply by , turning the sum into an average distance. On a directed graph you choose a direction: distances to measure how easily the graph reaches , distances from how easily reaches the graph. For importance on the web, distances to are the meaningful choice (see Centrality ). The unreachable-node problem If even one node cannot reach , the sum contains and closeness collapses to zero. On the web almost every pair is unreachable in one direction (see Paths, distance and reachability ), so the textbook formula assigns nearly every node zero. The usual repair sums only over nodes that can reach , and gives closeness 0 to nodes nothing reaches: That repair creates a new problem: a node reached by one neighbour at distance 1 gets closeness , the maximum possible, beating a node that the whole graph reaches in two or three steps. Worked example On the running example the repaired closeness gives: Node D F C A B G E Closeness 1 1 0.250 0.167 0.125 0.111 0 Nodes that reach it 1 1 4 4 4 5 0 D and F come first. Each is reached only by E, at distance 1. C, which every node with an out-link reaches, gets a quarter as much, because its sum of distances is over four nodes. G, reachable from more nodes than any other, ranks second to last. The measure rewards being hard to reach, as long as the few nodes that do reach you are close. The lab below lets you check: Lin’s index Nan Lin proposed in 1976 to weight closeness by how many nodes reach . With the number of nodes that can reach (counting itself), with the convention that a node nothing reaches scores 1. On a strongly connected graph for every node, so Lin’s index ranks exactly as closeness does. On the running example it gives C 6.25, A 4.17, then D, F and G tied at 4, B at 3.13 and E at 1. That is much more sensible, though the three-way tie still puts F level with G. Lin’s index satisfies the half of the size axiom but fails density and score monotonicity (see Axioms for centrality ). Axioms Closeness fails all three of Boldi and Vigna’s axioms: Size. In a graph made of a -clique and a separate -cycle, clique nodes score , which falls as the clique grows. Density. When a clique and a cycle of equal size are joined by one bidirectional arc, the cycle-side endpoint does not lose to the clique-side endpoint as it should. Score monotonicity. A new link to can lower its closeness. The link makes reachable from nodes that could not reach it before, and each adds a distance to the sum. Cost Exact closeness needs the distances from every node to every node: a breadth-first search from each node, in total. That is fine for a social network of a few thousand people and impossible for a web graph of a hundred million domains. Approximate methods sample sources, or count balls of growing radius with hyperloglog counters as hyperball does. Why harmonic centrality replaced it Replace the reciprocal of a sum of distances by a sum of reciprocals, and unreachable nodes contribute with no special case. That is Harmonic centrality , proposed for networks by Marchiori and Latora in 2000 and advocated by Boldi and Vigna as the measure that passes all three axioms. On a strongly connected graph harmonic and closeness centrality usually rank nodes similarly. On the web they do not, and harmonic is the one whose ranking makes sense. References Bavelas, A. (1950). Communication patterns in task-oriented groups. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 22(6), 725–730. Sabidussi, G. (1966). The centrality index of a graph. Psychometrika 31(4), 581–603. Lin, N. (1976). Foundations of Social Research . McGraw-Hill. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262.

d: Score each node by how many nodes link to it. The oldest, cheapest and most transparent centrality, and the one that "referring domains" reports.
a: In-degree centrality Prestige Popularity Citation count
x: Degree centrality ranks nodes by their Degree . On a directed link graph the meaningful version counts incoming arcs: a site is important if many sites link to it. It is what a citation count measures for a paper and what “referring domains” measures for a website. Every more elaborate measure in this encyclopedia can be read as a fix for one of its weaknesses. Definition The in-degree centrality of is sometimes divided by so that it lies between 0 and 1. Social network analysts call it prestige or popularity . The outgoing version, , measures activity : how many others a node points to. On the web, activity is free, so only in-degree carries information about how others see a site. Worked example In the running example, C receives four links, A two, and B, D, F and G one each; E receives none. Degree centrality ranks C first, A second, a four-way tie in third place and E last. The tie is the measure’s first visible weakness: G’s single link comes from C, the best-connected node, and F’s from E, which nothing links to, yet degree treats them identically. PageRank and Harmonic centrality both separate them (G scores 3 and F scores 1 under harmonic centrality). Strengths Cheap. One pass over the arcs, no iteration, no convergence threshold (see Degree ). Transparent. Anyone can verify an in-degree by listing the linking nodes. A centrality you can explain in one sentence is easier to trust and to audit. Monotone. Adding a link to always raises its score, and the measure satisfies the density axiom (see Axioms for centrality ). Strongly correlated with the rest. Across the 119,453 domains from the 2026-09-23 auction inventory that appear in Common Crawl’s graph, in-degree and harmonic centrality have a Spearman correlation of 0.69. For many purposes in-degree is a fair first approximation. Weaknesses Every link counts the same. A link from a national newspaper and a link from a site created yesterday add one each. This is the gap PageRank was designed to close. It is local. Degree sees only immediate neighbours. A site linked by three sites that are themselves linked by millions is, by degree, less important than one linked by four abandoned blogs. It is cheap to inflate. Manufacturing in-links needs only domains, and domains are cheap. A link farm of a thousand domains linking to a target adds a thousand to its in-degree. Recursive measures limit the damage, because the farm’s domains have little importance of their own to pass on. It fails half of the size axiom. Nodes on a long cycle always have in-degree 1, however large their community (see Axioms for centrality ). In-degree on the real web The top of Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph by in-degree: Domain Referring domains googleapis.com 17,119,122 facebook.com 16,967,941 google.com 16,347,517 gmpg.org 8,137,388 cloudflare.com 3,776,898 These numbers count every kind of reference Common Crawl extracts, including scripts, fonts and <link> elements, not only clickable anchors (see common-crawl-graph). gmpg.org illustrates the effect: WordPress themes have long included a <link rel="profile" href="https://gmpg.org/xfn/11"> element in every page header, so the site of a small 2003 microformat project receives links from more than 8 million domains. At the other end, the median domain has exactly one referring domain, and 12.4% have none. Among the auction domains that appear in the graph at all, the median in-degree is 1, the 90th percentile 5 and the 99th percentile 57. Degree in SEO tools Every link index reports in-degree in two forms (see backlinks): Backlinks count individual links, so a sitewide footer link on a 10,000-page site counts 10,000 times. Referring domains count distinct linking domains: the in-degree of the domain graph. Referring domains is the more robust of the two, but it inherits all of degree centrality’s weaknesses, and vendors’ counts include domains that link to almost everything. The metric-audit entry shows a floor of about 150 spam referring domains that one vendor reports for most listed auction domains, so a raw count below that floor says nothing at all. When degree is the right choice Use in-degree when you need a quick, explainable signal on a graph you trust, or as a sanity check on fancier scores. A domain whose PageRank is high but whose in-degree is tiny deserves a closer look, because a single strong link carries it, and the PageRank entry shows how fragile such scores are. When links may be manufactured, combine degree with a measure that weighs who links, such as Harmonic centrality , trustrank or spam-mass. References Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications . Cambridge University Press, chapter 5. Freeman, L. C. (1978). Centrality in social networks: conceptual clarification. Social Networks 1(3), 215–239. Garfield, E. (1972). Citation analysis as a tool in journal evaluation. Science 178(4060), 471–479.

d: In-degree counts the links a node receives and out-degree the links it makes; their distributions shape everything built on a link graph.
a: In-degree Out-degree Indegree Outdegree
x: Degree is the simplest thing you can measure about a node: how many arcs touch it. In a directed graph every node has two degrees. Its in-degree counts the arcs that point at it, and its out-degree counts the arcs it sends. On a domain graph, in-degree is the number of distinct domains that link to a domain, the quantity SEO tools call referring domains (see backlinks). Definition For a node in a directed graph : Each arc leaves one node and enters another, so the in-degrees and the out-degrees each sum to the number of arcs : and both average to . The averages agree, but the distributions do not. Popular sites collect in-links by the million, while out-degree tops out at whatever a site’s owner chooses to publish. Worked example In the running example (see the The web graph entry), the ten arcs give these degrees: Node A B C D E F G In-degree 2 1 4 1 0 1 1 Out-degree 2 1 2 2 3 0 0 Both rows sum to 10. C receives the most links, E sends the most and receives none, and F and G send none. A node with is a source ; a node with is a sink , which ranking algorithms call a dangling node. Degrees in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has 2,450,405,793 arcs among 119,722,885 domains, so both degrees average 20.47. The averages mislead badly: Statistic In-degree Out-degree Domains with degree 0 14,903,407 (12.4%) 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with degree 1 52,450,210 (43.8%) 7,021,336 (5.9%) Median 1 0 99th percentile 138 149 99.9th percentile 1,856 2,374 Largest 17,119,122 6,113,126 Share of all arcs held by the top 1% of domains 79.4% 78.6% The typical domain receives one link and sends none, while the top 1% of domains receive four in five of all links. That skew is the subject of the Degree distributions and power laws entry. The out-degree column says as much about the crawl as about the web. A domain the crawler never fetched has out-degree 0 whatever it links to in reality. The extremes are instructive. The largest in-degree belongs to googleapis.com , which serves fonts and scripts that millions of sites embed. The largest out-degree, 6,113,126, belongs to mp3fresh.net , a single domain that links to roughly one in twenty domains in the graph. No editorial process produces that many links; generated pages do. Extreme out-degree is a classic signal of link-spam. Computing degrees Degrees cost one pass over the arcs. Keep one counter per node, read each arc , and increment out[u] and in[v] . For the Common Crawl graph that means two arrays of 119.7 million 32-bit counters, 479 MB each, and a stream of 2.45 billion arcs. Reading the 9.4 GB gzipped edge list dominates: decompression takes a few minutes on one core, and the counting itself is noise. A compressed graph in the WebGraph format stores each node’s out-degree directly, so out-degrees come free; in-degrees need the transposed graph or one pass over the arcs. Degree as a measure of importance In-degree is the oldest ranking signal. Citation counts in science and “number of referring domains” in SEO are both in-degree. The Degree centrality entry examines it as a centrality measure: it is cheap, easy to explain and hard to fool at small scale, but it treats a link from a major newspaper and a link from a link farm as equal. PageRank and Harmonic centrality fix that by weighing who links, not only how many. Degree also feeds other measures. PageRank divides each node’s score among its out-links, so, per unit of the linker’s own score, a link from a node with out-degree 1 passes 6.1 million times more than a link from mp3fresh.net . assortativity asks whether high-degree nodes link to each other, and k-core decomposition peels a graph by degree. Weighted degree Collapsing parallel links throws away counts. A page graph knows that one domain links to another 5,000 times across its pages; a domain graph keeps one arc. Tools that report “backlinks” count the raw links, while “referring domains” counts the distinct linking domains, which is the domain graph’s in-degree. The two differ by orders of magnitude for sites with sitewide footer links, which is why referring domains is the better-behaved number (see backlinks). References Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications . Cambridge University Press, chapter 4. Broder, A., et al. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320.

d: A node's score is proportional to the sum of the scores of the nodes linking to it. The cleanest form of "important nodes are those linked by important nodes", and the parent of PageRank.
a: Eigenvector Bonacich centrality Dominant eigenvector
x: Eigenvector centrality takes the recursive idea of importance literally: each node’s score is proportional to the total score of the nodes that link to it. Phillip Bonacich formalised it for social networks in 1972. The scores form an eigenvector of the Adjacency matrices and lists matrix, hence the name. The idea is elegant, and on strongly connected graphs it works. On web graphs it breaks in instructive ways, and Katz centrality and PageRank are best understood as repairs. Definition Ask for a vector with is an eigenvector of with eigenvalue . Eigenvector centrality takes the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, the spectral radius , scaled to sum to 1 (or to have unit length; only ratios matter). The perron-frobenius theorem says that this eigenvector can be chosen with no negative entries, and that it is unique and strictly positive when the graph is strongly connected. Compared with in-degree, the change is one word: a link counts with the score of its source instead of counting as 1. Compared with PageRank, two things are missing: the source’s score is not divided among its out-links, and there is no teleportation. Worked example On the running example the dominant eigenvalue is , and the scores are: Node C A G B D E F Eigenvector centrality 0.325 0.245 0.245 0.185 0 0 0 The eigenvalue has a neat origin. Inside the core, , and . Substituting gives , whose real root is the so-called plastic number, 1.3247. The core’s two cycles, of lengths 2 and 3, set the growth rate. The zeros are the important part. D, E and F score exactly 0, though D and E link into the core and D even has an in-link. Nothing in the core can reach them, and the equation propagates scores only forward from the core. E has no in-links, so ; D’s only in-link comes from E, so too; and F likewise. G, downstream of C, scores exactly as much as A, since each receives a link from one core node with the same equation. Where it breaks Zero outside the dominant component. On a graph that is not strongly connected, every node that the dominant strongly connected component cannot reach scores zero. On the web, that means most of the IN set of the The bow-tie structure and everything hanging off it. No dilution by out-degree. A node with a million out-links passes its full score along each one. Hubs inflate the scores of everything they touch, and a link farm whose members link densely to each other can build a large eigenvalue of its own and capture the whole vector. Localisation. On large graphs with heavy-tailed degrees, the dominant eigenvector tends to concentrate on the highest-degree node and its immediate neighbours, giving vanishing scores to everyone else. Martin, Zhang and Newman showed this in 2014 and proposed a non-backtracking variant to avoid it. Periodicity. Computing the vector by power-iteration fails to converge on graphs whose cycles all share a common length divisor; the iterates oscillate. The running example is safe because its core has cycles of lengths 2 and 3. In Boldi and Vigna’s Axioms for centrality eigenvector centrality satisfies density, only the half of size, and fails score monotonicity. The repairs Each fix addresses one failure: Katz centrality adds a constant to every node: . Every node gets a baseline, so nodes outside the core no longer vanish. PageRank divides each node’s score among its out-links, which tames hubs, and adds teleportation, which makes the graph strongly connected and aperiodic in effect. Its scores come from the stationary distribution of a random walk instead of the adjacency matrix itself. hits splits the role of a node in two, hub and authority, and takes eigenvectors of and . PageRank’s success on the web is largely the success of these repairs. Computing it Power iteration multiplies a vector by and renormalises until it stops changing. Each iteration costs one pass over the arcs; the number of iterations depends on the ratio between the two largest eigenvalue moduli, , which on real graphs can be close to 1. Unlike PageRank, nothing bounds this ratio, so convergence can be slow. Where it is used Eigenvector centrality is common in social network analysis on small, connected networks such as friendship or trade networks, where its assumptions hold. On web-scale link graphs, practitioners use its repaired descendants. Knowing the raw form remains useful: when a spectral metric gives exact zeros or wildly concentrated scores, the failure modes above are usually the reason. References Bonacich, P. (1972). Factoring and weighting approaches to status scores and clique identification. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 2(1), 113–120. Bonacich, P. (1987). Power and centrality: A family of measures. American Journal of Sociology 92(5), 1170–1182. Martin, T., Zhang, X., & Newman, M. E. J. (2014). Localization and centrality in networks. Physical Review E 90(5), 052808.

d: The same links give three different graphs depending on whether a node is a URL, a host name or a registered domain. Each level answers different questions and hides different problems.
a: Host graph Domain graph Page graph Granularity
x: A link joins two URLs, but a link graph can treat its nodes at three levels of detail. In a page graph every URL is a node. In a host graph every host name ( blog.example.com , www.example.com ) is a node, and every link between pages on two different hosts becomes an arc between those hosts. In a domain graph every registered domain ( example.com , example.co.uk ) is a node, and all its hosts merge into it. Moving up a level shrinks the graph by orders of magnitude and changes what the rankings mean. Folding one level into the next Going from pages to hosts, or from hosts to domains, is a quotient : replace each node by the group it belongs to, keep one arc between two groups if any arc joined their members, and drop arcs inside a group. Map every URL to its host name, lower-cased. Map every host to its registered domain using the Public Suffix List, so that a.example.co.uk maps to example.co.uk , not to co.uk (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). Collapse parallel arcs and drop self-loops. Step 3 discards most links. All internal navigation (a site’s menus, pagination, related-article blocks) links pages of the same host and disappears at the host level. Links between a domain’s own hosts, such as shop.example.com → www.example.com , disappear at the domain level. Common Crawl’s host-level extraction keeps only links between different hosts to begin with. The three levels compared Page graph Host graph Domain graph Node URL host name registered domain Typical size of a large crawl billions of nodes, tens to hundreds of billions of arcs hundreds of millions of nodes, billions of arcs about 120 million nodes, a few billion arcs Keeps internal linking yes no no Separates subdomains yes yes no Natural question which page answers a query? which site is important? which registrable name is important? Common Crawl publishes host-level and domain-level graphs. Its 2026 domain graph has 119,722,885 domains folded from the host graph; the n_hosts column of its ranks file says how many hosts went into each domain. The hosts average 1.96 per domain, about 235 million in total, and 90,515,169 domains (75.6%) consist of a single host. What merging hides Folding hosts into domains is right for most sites, where www.example.com and example.com are one organisation. It is wrong for platforms that give each customer a host of their own: blogspot.com folds 4,113,910 hosts, each a separate blog, into one node. wordpress.com folds 1,958,600 hosts. googleapis.com includes storage.googleapis.com , where Google Cloud Storage serves whatever files its customers upload. At the domain level, every link to any blog on blogspot.com counts toward one node, and every link from any customer page counts as a link from the platform. The PageRank entry shows a consequence: chaussurespuma.net sits at PageRank position 10,000 because of a single link credited to googleapis.com , whatever page actually carries it. Hosting pages on a reputable shared domain to borrow its standing is a recognised spam tactic, and the domain graph rewards it. What splitting hides The host level has the opposite problem. A site that moves from www.example.com to example.com , or spreads content across shop. , blog. and help. hosts, splits its in-links across several nodes. A host graph then underrates it, while the domain graph sums the pieces. Many sites also link heavily between their own hosts, which a host graph counts as external links and a domain graph rightly drops. Choosing a level Search ranking needs pages, because queries are answered by pages. Google’s original PageRank ran on the page graph. Crawl prioritisation works well at the host level, which is the unit of politeness for crawlers. Common Crawl ranks hosts by Harmonic centrality to decide what to fetch next. Domain valuation needs the domain level, because a registered domain is the asset that changes hands. When you buy example.com you get every host under it, including links pointing at a long-dead forum.example.com (see expired-domains). Commercial link indexes report both levels. Ahrefs’ URL Rating and Moz’s Page Authority score pages; domain-rating and domain-authority score domains. The same backlink appears in both, so a strong page on a weak domain and a weak page on a strong domain look different depending on which number you read. Granularity changes rankings The same crawl ranked at different levels gives different answers, and none of them is the “true” one. A popular blog on blogspot.com is a top host in the host graph but invisible in the domain graph, where blogspot.com itself takes the credit. When you compare a domain’s rank across sources, check that they measured the same kind of node: a host-level rank for www.example.com and a domain-level rank for example.com are not the same quantity. Mozilla Foundation. Public Suffix List. publicsuffix.org. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602.

d: Add up one over the distance from every other node. Nodes that the whole graph reaches in few steps score high, unreachable nodes simply count zero, and link farms gain almost nothing.
a: Harmonic Harmonic closeness hc harmonicc
x: Harmonic centrality scores a node by summing the reciprocals of the distances to it from every other node. A node at distance 1 adds 1, a node at distance 2 adds ½, a node at distance 3 adds ⅓, and a node that cannot reach it adds nothing. It fixes the flaw that makes Closeness centrality useless on the web, it is the only classical measure that passes all three of Boldi and Vigna’s Axioms for centrality , and it is one of the two rankings Common Crawl publishes for every host and domain. Definition For a node in a directed graph, Grouping nodes by distance gives an equivalent form. If is the number of nodes at distance exactly from which can be reached, so the first term is the in-degree. Harmonic centrality is in-degree plus a discounted count of everyone further away. Dividing by scales it to , with 1 meaning every other node links directly to . Marchiori and Latora introduced the harmonic mean of distances for networks in 2000, Rochat proposed it as a centrality for disconnected graphs in 2009, and Boldi and Vigna’s 2014 analysis made the case for it as the geometric centrality. Worked example On the running example: Node C A G B D F E Harmonic centrality 4 3 3 2.33 1 1 0 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C scores 4: A, B, D and E each link to it directly. G scores 3 from a single in-link, because almost the whole graph reaches it in two steps: from C plus each from A, B, D and E. D and F score 1 each, from E alone. Compare Closeness centrality , which ranks D and F first on the same graph. Why it behaves well Unreachable nodes need no special case. They contribute zero, so the formula works unchanged on graphs that are not strongly connected, which is every real web graph. It satisfies all three axioms. Size: a clique node scores while a cycle node scores the harmonic number , so either side wins once large enough. Density: the clique side of a bridge beats the cycle side. Score monotonicity: a new arc shortens or creates distances to and can never lengthen one, so rises (see Axioms for centrality ). It rewards reach, not concentration. Unlike PageRank , it does not care how a linking node splits its attention. A link from a site with a million out-links helps exactly as much as a link from a site with one. Why link farms gain almost nothing Suppose a spammer registers 1,000 fresh domains, each linking only to a target that had no in-links. Nothing links to the farm domains, so each contributes exactly 1 to the target’s harmonic centrality, for a total of 1,000. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph a harmonic value of 1,000 sits below position 100,000,000 of 119.7 million; the domain at position 100 million already scores 7.4 million. Under PageRank the same farm is worth far more. Each farm domain holds the graph’s floor score of and passes 85% of it to the target, so 1,000 of them deliver about . That is the PageRank of the domain at position 10,000. The same thousand cheap domains that move a target from nowhere to the top ten thousand under PageRank leave it in the bottom fifth under harmonic centrality. To score well, a domain must be close to a large share of the whole web, and only links from well-reached domains provide that. Common Crawl ranks hosts by harmonic centrality to prioritise its crawl largely for this reason (see link-spam). Computing it at scale Exact harmonic centrality needs a breadth-first search from every node on the transposed graph, in total, about steps for Common Crawl’s domain graph. Nobody computes it exactly at that scale. The hyperball algorithm computes it approximately. It keeps one HyperLogLog counter per node estimating the size of the ball of nodes within distance , and grows every ball by one step per pass over the graph. The harmonic centrality is then The passes stop when no counter changes, which takes as many passes as the longest shortest path in the graph. Common Crawl runs WebGraph’s HyperBall on the transposed graph, with counters kept on disk ( --offline ), to produce the #harmonicc_val column of its ranks files. The approximation shows in the data. Of the 119.7 million domains, only 5,940,987 distinct harmonic values occur, and 14,903,700 domains have value 0. That is 293 more than the 14,903,407 domains with no in-links: for a few domains with a single in-link, the counters missed it. Treat harmonic values as estimates with a few percent of relative error, and differences in the last digits as noise. Reading Common Crawl’s harmonic values Position Harmonic value Example 1 28,819,640 googleapis.com 100 19,303,032 reuters.com 10,000 16,972,598 amctheatres.com 100,000 16,485,265 1,000,000 13,857,260 10,000,000 12,448,198 100,000,000 7,444,818 104,819,186 onward 0 14.9 million domains The values crowd together. Position 100,000 still scores 57% of the top value, and position 10 million 43%. Small differences in value therefore become enormous differences in position: wixstatic.com and parastorage.com each receive links from about three million domains and differ in harmonic value by 18%, yet they sit at positions 26 and 81,305. When you compare two domains, compare values or log-ratios, not positions (see ranks-and-scores). googleapis.com ’s value has a direct reading: its 17.1 million referring domains contribute 17.1 million, and the remaining 11.7 million comes from domains two or more steps away. Closeness centrality extended to unconnected graphs: the harmonic centrality index. Applications of Social Network Analysis (ASNA) 2009 . Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2013). In-core computation of geometric centralities with HyperBall: A hundred billion nodes and beyond. ICDM Workshops 2013 , 621–628.

d: Count every walk that ends at a node, weighting a walk of length k by β to the power k. Short walks count most, everyone gets a baseline, and one parameter slides the measure from in-degree to eigenvector centrality.
a: Katz Katz index Attenuation factor Alpha centrality
x: Leo Katz proposed in 1953 to measure a person’s status by counting not only who chooses them directly but also who chooses those people, and so on, with each extra step counting less. On a link graph, Katz centrality counts every walk that ends at a node, weighting walks of length by for some attenuation factor . It sits between Degree centrality , which counts walks of length 1, and Eigenvector centrality , which it approaches as grows. It also fixes eigenvector centrality’s habit of giving most of the web a score of zero. Definition Since counts the walks of length from to (see Adjacency matrices and lists ), the number of length- walks ending at each node is the vector . Katz centrality sums them with geometric weights: The series converges if and only if , where is the largest eigenvalue of . Rearranging gives a recursive form that shows the connection to eigenvector centrality: Each in-link contributes its source’s score plus one . The “+1” is the whole difference from eigenvector centrality: every node passes on at least a baseline, so nodes outside the dominant strongly connected component no longer vanish. The two limits As , walks of length 1 dominate, and the ranking converges to in-degree. As , long walks dominate, the series grows without bound, and the ranking converges to eigenvector centrality. Between the limits, is a dial between local popularity and global, recursive prestige. Bonacich’s alpha centrality and PageRank both belong to the same family, differing in what they add to each node and whether they divide by out-degree. Worked example The running example’s largest eigenvalue is 1.3247, so must stay below . With : Node C A G B D F E Katz () 1.868 1.250 0.860 0.675 0.300 0.300 0 Eigenvector 0.325 0.245 0.245 0.185 0 0 0 D and F each receive one walk of length 1, from E, and nothing longer, since nothing reaches E: their score is exactly . Unlike eigenvector centrality, Katz separates A from G: A gets walks from inside the core, G only through C. Drag β towards 0.75 in the lab and watch the scores explode as the series approaches divergence: Axioms Katz satisfies density and score monotonicity, and the half of the size axiom (see Axioms for centrality ). Adding a link adds new walks into and removes none, so ’s score always rises. In that respect Katz behaves better than eigenvector centrality and as well as PageRank . Computing it The recursive form gives an iteration: start from and repeat . Each step costs one pass over the arcs and the error shrinks by a factor of about per step. Alternatively, solve the sparse linear system with Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel iterations, as for PageRank (see pagerank-linear-system). The trouble with β on the web The admissible range of depends on , and on a web graph that number is set by its densest corner. The spectral radius of a graph is at least the smallest in-degree inside any of its subgraphs, counting only arcs within the subgraph. One cluster of a few thousand domains that all link to each other therefore pushes into the thousands and forces below for the whole graph. With that small, Katz centrality is in-degree plus a rounding error everywhere outside the cluster. On a graph full of link farms, the farms decide the parameter. PageRank avoids this by dividing each node’s score among its out-links, which caps the spectral radius of its matrix at 1. Where it is used Katz centrality and its relative, the Katz index between pairs of nodes, are popular in social network analysis and in link prediction, where the weighted count of walks between two nodes predicts future links between them. In web ranking it is mostly of historical and conceptual importance: it showed in 1953 how to count indirect endorsements with decay, an idea PageRank refined forty-five years later. References Katz, L. (1953). A new status index derived from sociometric analysis. Psychometrika 18(1), 39–43. Bonacich, P., & Lloyd, P. (2001). Eigenvector-like measures of centrality for asymmetric relations. Social Networks 23(3), 191–201. Vigna, S. (2016). Spectral ranking. Network Science 4(4), 433–445.

d: A node is important if important nodes link to it. PageRank makes that circular idea precise as the long-run behaviour of a random surfer who sometimes gets bored and jumps.
a: PR Google PageRank
x: PageRank scores every node of a link graph by the fraction of time a random surfer spends there. The surfer starts anywhere, follows a random out-link at each step, and every so often jumps to a random node instead. Sites that many well-visited sites link to get visited often. Larry Page and Sergey Brin introduced it in 1998 as the ranking core of the Google search engine, and it remains the reference point that every other link-based ranking is compared against. The idea Counting in-links ( Degree centrality ) treats every link as equal. PageRank adds two rules: A link from an important node counts more. Importance flows along links. A node splits its importance among its out-links. A site that links to a thousand others passes each one a thousandth of what a site linking to one passes. The definition is circular, since importance depends on importance. The random-surfer model resolves the circularity: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk , the distribution that one more step of the walk leaves unchanged. Definition Let be the number of nodes, the out-degree of , and the damping-factor, conventionally 0.85. The PageRank vector satisfies, for every node , Read it term by term. With probability the surfer teleports to a uniformly random node. With probability it follows a link: each in-neighbour sends an equal share of its own score. The last sum handles dangling-nodes: a surfer stuck on a node with no out-links teleports uniformly. The scores are positive and sum to 1. In matrix form, with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix (dangling rows replaced by the uniform row) and the all-ones vector, The perron-frobenius theorem guarantees exactly one solution, and power-iteration finds it by applying the right-hand side repeatedly. The error shrinks by a factor of about per iteration. Personalized PageRank replaces the uniform teleport with any other distribution. Worked example On the running example with , power iteration converges to a change below after 43 iterations: Node C A G B D F E PageRank 0.2977 0.2052 0.1774 0.1381 0.0653 0.0653 0.0509 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C wins, as in-degree predicts. The surprises are lower down: G beats B, though both have one in-link. G’s link comes from C, the top node, which splits its score two ways. B’s comes from A, which has a lower score and also splits two ways. E gets the minimum. Nothing links to E, so it receives only the teleport share plus its share of the dangling mass: . Every node with no in-links in any graph gets exactly this floor. D and F tie. Each has a single in-link from E, which splits three ways: . Try it yourself. Change α or add a link from G back to E, and watch E climb: Properties worth knowing Scores are probabilities. They sum to 1, so they shrink as the graph grows. On a graph of 120 million nodes, the average score is . Compare positions, or logarithms, not raw values (see ranks-and-scores). Adding an in-link always helps. In Boldi and Vigna’s terms PageRank satisfies score monotonicity : adding an arc raises ’s score. It fails their size axiom, though: in a graph made of one large clique and one long cycle, every node scores exactly , so PageRank cannot tell a big community from a small one (see Axioms for centrality ). Small α flattens, large α concentrates. With the running example’s range shrinks from 0.05–0.30 to 0.09–0.24. As the scores pile into the strongly connected core and convergence slows (see damping-factor). It can be farmed. A group of sites that link to each other and to a target trap the random surfer and pump the target’s score. trustrank, spam-mass and Harmonic centrality all respond to this weakness (see link-spam). At web scale Each power iteration reads every arc once and updates a score vector of entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph that is 2.45 billion arcs and two vectors of 119.7 million doubles (958 MB each). Common Crawl runs the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver on the transposed graph, which converges in fewer passes than plain power iteration (see pagerank-linear-system). pagerank-at-scale works through the memory budget, and monte-carlo-pagerank and push-algorithms approximate scores without touching the whole graph. PageRank on the real web In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph the top of the PageRank list is the infrastructure every site embeds: googleapis.com (0.0152), google.com (0.0151), facebook.com (0.0094), googletagmanager.com and instagram.com . The common ranking with Harmonic centrality diverges further down, and the divergence shows what PageRank rewards: Domain Referring domains PageRank position Harmonic position godaddy.com 1,472,755 14 135 parastorage.com 2,923,364 16 81,305 miit.gov.cn 722,788 28 981 PageRank pays most for links from sites that link to little else, because each such link carries a large share of its source’s score. godaddy.com is linked from parked pages and from sites built with its tools, and miit.gov.cn from the registration notice that Chinese sites display. Harmonic centrality ignores how a source splits its links and only asks how close the rest of the graph is. The extreme case sits further down. chaussurespuma.net has seven referring domains, yet it holds PageRank position 10,000 of 119.7 million. One of the seven is googleapis.com , the top domain, which links to only 3,686 domains. That single link passes , almost all of chaussurespuma.net ’s score of . Google Cloud Storage serves user files from storage.googleapis.com , so the link may sit on a page any customer uploaded; the domain graph credits it to googleapis.com all the same (see Page, host and domain graphs ). What it means for a domain Google’s production ranking has used many signals beyond PageRank for decades, and its link analysis runs on pages, not domains, with spam filtering and link-attributes applied. A domain graph’s PageRank is a useful, reproducible proxy for one question: how much of the web’s link attention flows to this domain

d: How many clicks separate two sites, and whether one can reach the other at all. Breadth-first search answers both, and geometric centralities are built on the answer.
a: Distance Shortest path Reachability Breadth-first search BFS Geodesic
x: A path from to is a sequence of arcs that starts at , follows links, and ends at . The distance is the length of the shortest such path, counted in arcs. On the web it is the minimum number of clicks a reader needs to get from one site to another. If no path exists, is unreachable from and . Distances matter because a family of rankings, the geometric centralities, score a node by how close the rest of the graph is to it: Closeness centrality , Harmonic centrality and Betweenness centrality , which counts how many shortest paths pass through a node. Distance is not symmetric In a directed graph and can differ, and one can be infinite while the other is not. In the running example, through C, but : G links nowhere and nothing links to E. Here is every distance in the running example. Row , column gives ; a dash means unreachable. from \ to A B C D E F G A 0 1 1 – – – 2 B 2 0 1 – – – 2 C 1 2 0 – – – 1 D 1 2 1 0 – – 2 E 2 3 1 1 0 1 2 F – – – – – 0 – G – – – – – – 0 Most of the table is dashes. Unreachable pairs are the norm in web graphs, not an edge case, and any measure built on distance must decide what to do with them. Closeness centrality handles them badly and Harmonic centrality handles them well, which is the main reason the second replaced the first. Reachability The set of nodes reachable from is its forward ball of infinite radius; the set of nodes that can reach is its backward ball . Reachability decomposes a graph into strongly connected components : groups in which every node reaches every other. On the web those components arrange themselves into the The bow-tie structure shape. In the running example, E reaches everything, while F and G reach only themselves. Column C is full except for F and G: every node that links anywhere eventually reaches C. Breadth-first search Breadth-first search (BFS) computes all distances from one source in time proportional to the number of arcs it touches: dist[s] = 0; queue = [s] while queue not empty: u = queue.pop_front() for v in successors(u): if dist[v] is unset: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 queue.push_back(v) BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches it has found a shortest path. Each arc is examined once, so one BFS costs . Running BFS on the transposed graph (see Adjacency matrices and lists ) gives the distances to from everywhere, which is what in-link-based centralities need. All-pairs distances are out of reach A geometric centrality needs the distances between all pairs, which naively means one BFS per node: . For Common Crawl’s domain graph, with and , that is about arc visits. At a billion visits per second it would take nearly ten years. Two ideas make geometric centralities feasible at that scale anyway: Approximate counting. You rarely need every distance, only how many nodes lie within distance for each . HyperBall estimates those counts for every node at once with HyperLogLog counters, in a few dozen passes over the graph. Common Crawl computes Harmonic centrality this way. Sampling. Run BFS from a random sample of sources and extrapolate. This is how large-scale betweenness is usually estimated (see brandes-algorithm). Diameter and typical distance The diameter is the largest finite distance between any two nodes. It is a fragile statistic: one long chain of pages sets it. Network scientists prefer the distance distribution , the fraction of reachable pairs at each distance, and the effective diameter , the distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie. Web graphs and social networks have small typical distances, the small-world property, and the neighbourhood-function entry shows how to measure the whole distribution at scale. On Facebook’s 2011 friendship graph, 721 million users were on average 4.74 friendships apart, a figure computed with HyperANF. Weighted distance When arcs carry lengths, BFS gives way to Dijkstra’s algorithm, which costs with a good priority queue. Link graphs rarely use weighted distances; the meaningful weights on links, such as how much importance they transfer, enter through Random walks and Markov chains instead. References Cormen, T. Four degrees of separation. WebSci 2012 , 33–42.

d: PageRank with the random surfer's jumps aimed at chosen nodes instead of anywhere. It measures importance from a point of view, and underlies TrustRank, topic-sensitive search and local graph clustering.
a: PPR Topic-sensitive PageRank Random walk with restart Preference vector
x: Ordinary PageRank teleports the random surfer to a uniformly random node. Personalized PageRank (PPR) teleports it according to a chosen preference vector instead: always to one node, or to a handful of trusted sites, or to pages about one topic. The resulting scores measure importance as seen from the preferred nodes: nodes that the walk reaches often, after restarting at the preferred nodes, score high. The original PageRank paper already described this variant; it later became the basis of trustrank, of topic-sensitive search, and of fast local algorithms for finding communities. Definition Given a probability vector over the nodes, the personalized PageRank vector satisfies with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix and the damping-factor. A walker at each step follows a random out-link with probability and jumps to a node drawn from with probability . From a dangling node it jumps according to as well (“strongly preferential”) or uniformly (“weakly preferential”). With uniform, is ordinary PageRank. When puts all its mass on a single node , the walk is a random walk with restart , and measures how close is to : it is the probability that a walk from with geometric length, mean steps, ends at . Worked example Restart every walk at E in the running example, with : Node E C A G D F B PPR from E 0.307 0.230 0.135 0.098 0.087 0.087 0.057 Ordinary PageRank 0.051 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.065 0.065 0.138 E, which has the lowest ordinary PageRank, now has the highest score, because every restart lands on it. B drops to last: it is three links away from E, the farthest node E can reach. The ranking now mixes importance with proximity to the seed. Pick a different seed in the lab to see the whole ranking shift: Linearity PPR is linear in the preference vector: if , then . Two consequences matter in practice: Topic-sensitive PageRank. Haveliwala precomputed one PPR vector for each of the 16 top-level categories of the Open Directory, each teleporting to that category’s pages. At query time he mixed the 16 vectors according to how well the query matched each topic. One query about jaguars the animal and another about Jaguar the car get different link-based rankings from the same 16 vectors. Personalization at scale. In principle, the PPR vector of every single node determines the PPR of every possible preference vector. Storing vectors of length is impossible on the web, but Jeh and Widom showed how to share most of the work through a small set of hub nodes, and Monte Carlo methods store a few walk endpoints per node instead (see monte-carlo-pagerank). Computing it Power iteration works exactly as for PageRank, one pass over the arcs per iteration, but it computes one preference vector at a time. Local push algorithms compute an approximate PPR from a single seed while touching only the nodes near it, in time independent of the graph’s size (see push-algorithms). Andersen, Chung and Lang used this to find communities: sort nodes by PPR score divided by degree and cut where the conductance is lowest. Monte Carlo estimation runs many random walks with restart from the seed and counts where they stop. Where it is used Spam resistance. trustrank is PPR with the preference vector on a hand-checked set of reputable sites. Spam pages are rarely close to such seeds. spam-mass compares ordinary PageRank with this trusted version. Recommendation. “Who to follow” and “related items” features rank candidates by PPR from the user. Twitter’s original Who-to-Follow service, described by Gupta and colleagues in 2013, combined personalized PageRank with SALSA on the follow graph. Local search and clustering. PPR from one node finds the cluster around it without processing the whole graph. Link analysis for a niche. Seeding the walk with the leading sites of one industry ranks domains by their standing within that industry rather than on the web at large. Majestic’s Topical Trust Flow reports a separate link-based score for each topic category, in the same spirit (see trust-flow). What it means for a domain A domain’s ordinary PageRank says how much of the web’s link attention it gets. A personalized score says how much attention it gets from the part of the web you care about. A domain with modest overall PageRank but strong PPR from authoritative sites in one field can be worth more, for that field, than a domain with high overall PageRank earned from unrelated or low-quality sources. d: Most sites receive almost no links and a few receive millions. That heavy tail explains why link metrics live on logarithmic scales and why averages mislead.
a: Power law Heavy tail Scale-free Degree distribution Pareto distribution Zipf's law
x: A graph’s degree distribution says what fraction of nodes have each degree. In a random graph where every link lands on a uniformly chosen node, degrees cluster tightly around the average. Link graphs look nothing like that. Most nodes have tiny degrees and a few have degrees millions of times larger. When the fraction of nodes with degree falls off like a power of , the distribution is called a power law and the graph scale-free . Whether real web graphs follow a true power law is debated; that they are extremely heavy-tailed is not. Definition A degree distribution follows a power law with exponent if, for above some threshold , Equivalently, the share of nodes with degree at least , the complementary cumulative distribution (CCDF), falls like . Taking logarithms turns either into a straight line, , which is why power laws are plotted on log–log axes. The CCDF is the better plot: it needs no binning and its tail is not lost in noise. The exponent controls how extreme the tail is. For the variance diverges as the graph grows, and for even the mean does: a handful of nodes then hold a fixed fraction of all links, however many nodes there are.
