Both axes are logarithmic. Both curves fall roughly as straight lines over several orders of magnitude. Reading off the in-degree curve: In-degree at least Domains Share 1 104,819,478 87.6% 10 11,197,454 9.4% 100 1,603,071 1.3% 1,000 222,959 0.19% 10,000 44,463 0.037% 100,000 334 0.0003% 1,000,000 45 10,000,000 5 Between 10 and 10,000 links, each tenfold rise in degree divides the count by about seven: a straight line on the plot. Then the line shows a shelf and a cliff. About 39,400 domains have in-degree between 19,000 and 29,000, where the smooth tail predicts fewer than 2,000, and out-degrees show a matching bump between 22,000 and 38,000. The natural reading is one network of tens of thousands of domains that each link to most of the others: the signature of a link farm, or of a large group of sites that share a sitewide footer. Past the bump the tail resumes, with 334 domains above 100,000 in-links and 5 above ten million. Fitting the tail by maximum likelihood gives an exponent of for in-degrees of at least 10, drifting up to 1.92 for in-degrees of at least 1,000. Out-degrees give similar values (1.84 to 1.99). Exponents below 2 match what the totals say directly: the top 1% of domains receive 79.4% of all links, and the top 0.1% receive 61.0%. Page-level graphs measured in earlier studies give steeper tails. Broder and colleagues reported for in-degree and 2.72 for out-degree on 203 million pages; Barabási and Albert reported 2.1 and 2.45 on the nd.edu domain in 1999. Domain graphs concentrate further because one domain collects the links aimed at all its pages. Fit carefully The straight line on a log–log plot is famously easy to over-read: Do not fit a line to a log–log histogram. Least squares on binned, logged counts gives biased exponents and no test of fit. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman recommend maximum likelihood instead: for discrete data, over the nodes with , plus a goodness-of-fit test against alternatives such as the lognormal. The tail is not the whole distribution. Below about 10 links the CC curve bends; 43.8% of domains have exactly one in-link and 63.8% have no recorded out-link at all, the latter mostly an artefact of what the crawler fetched. Heavy-tailed is not the same as power law. Meusel, Vigna and colleagues tested the in-degree distribution of Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph and rejected a power law, though the tail is unmistakably heavy. The subtitle of their paper, “a trick of the heavy tail”, is the point: many distributions look straight on log–log axes over a few decades. Where heavy tails come from The classic explanation is preferential attachment : new sites link to existing sites with probability proportional to how many links those sites already have, so the rich get richer. Barabási and Albert showed that this rule alone produces a power law with exponent 3; variants with copying or aging produce other exponents. Search engines may strengthen the effect, since sites that rank well get found, and then linked, more often. The random-graph-models entry compares the main models. Why it matters for rankings and metrics Averages mislead. The mean in-degree is 20.5 but the median is 1. Any summary of link metrics should use medians, percentiles or logarithms. Scores need logarithmic scales. Proprietary metrics such as domain-rating and domain-authority map raw link signals onto 0–100 scales that their vendors describe as logarithmic: moving from 70 to 80 is far harder than from 20 to 30. The old Toolbar PageRank used a 0–10 log scale (see pagerank-history). Most domains sit at the floor. Any link metric piles a large share of domains onto its minimum value. Among the 2026-09-23 auction domains, 89% are absent from Common Crawl’s graph altogether (see metric-audit). Hubs dominate computation. A node with 17 million in-links makes load balancing in parallel algorithms hard and shapes the compression of the graph (see webgraph-compression). References Barabási, A.-L., & Albert, R. (1999). d: A walker who follows random links visits some nodes more often than others. The long-run visit frequencies, the stationary distribution, are the mathematical core of PageRank and its relatives.
a: Random walk Markov chain Stationary distribution Transition matrix Ergodic
x: A random walk on a graph starts at some node and, at every step, moves along an out-link chosen uniformly at random. Run it for a long time and count how often it visits each node. On a well-behaved graph those frequencies settle down to a fixed distribution, the stationary distribution , which no longer depends on where the walk started. Nodes that many frequently visited nodes link to get visited often. That is the idea behind PageRank , and the theory of Markov chains says when it works. Transition matrix Write for the matrix with when links to and 0 otherwise, the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix. Row is the probability distribution of the walker’s next position when it stands on . If is a row vector giving the probability of being at each node after steps, then A stationary distribution is a probability vector that one step leaves unchanged: Each node’s stationary probability equals the probability flowing into it: . That is the PageRank equation without the teleport term. A small example Take only the core of the running example: A links to B and C, B links to C, and C links to A. The transition probabilities are and . Solving : With the probabilities summing to 1, . The walker spends 40% of its time on A, 40% on C and 20% on B. B loses because it receives only half of A’s traffic, while C receives the other half plus everything from B. When a unique answer exists Markov chain theory gives two conditions: Irreducible. Every node can reach every other, so the graph is one strongly connected component . Then exactly one stationary distribution exists, and it is positive everywhere. Aperiodic. The lengths of the graph’s cycles have greatest common divisor 1. Then converges to from any starting distribution. In a graph whose only cycles have length 2 (A ⇄ B), a walker starting on A is on A at every even step forever, and oscillates instead of settling. The core above has a cycle of length 2 (A → C → A) and one of length 3 (A → B → C → A), so it is aperiodic, and converges to . A chain that is both irreducible and aperiodic is called ergodic . The perron-frobenius theorem is the linear-algebra version of this result. Why the raw web breaks both conditions The web graph is neither irreducible nor safe to walk on: Dangling nodes. A node with no out-links has an empty row in . A walker who lands there has nowhere to go, and probability leaks out of the system. In Common Crawl’s domain graph, 63.8% of nodes are dangling (see dangling-nodes). Traps. Groups of nodes with links in but no links out, such as the OUT part of the The bow-tie structure , absorb the walker forever. The stationary distribution of the raw walk puts all its mass in such traps and gives zero to everything else, including the core. PageRank repairs both with teleportation : with probability the walker jumps to a random node, and from a dangling node it always jumps. The repaired chain is irreducible and aperiodic by construction, so it has a unique stationary distribution, which is the PageRank vector (see random-surfer and damping-factor). Undirected graphs are easy On an undirected graph the stationary distribution has a closed form: , proportional to degree. A random walk on an undirected graph is therefore just a slow way to compute Degree centrality . Direction is what makes random walks interesting on the web: a link from to sends traffic one way only, and the stationary distribution depends on the whole structure of who links to whom. How fast the walk forgets its start The mixing time is how many steps it takes for to get close to . It is governed by the second-largest eigenvalue modulus of the transition matrix: the distance to shrinks roughly like . For PageRank’s repaired matrix, Haveliwala and Kamvar showed that , which is why power-iteration converges in a predictable number of steps however large the graph is. Variants used in link analysis Random walk with restart. The walker teleports back to one fixed node, or a small set, instead of anywhere. Its stationary distribution is Personalized PageRank , a measure of proximity to the restart set, and the basis of trustrank. Backward walks. Walking along in-links instead of out-links scores nodes by what they link to . That gives cheirank. Alternating walks. Stepping forward along a link and then backward along another gives salsa, a stochastic version of hits. Simulated walks. Instead of solving equations, run many short walks and count where they end. monte-carlo-pagerank estimates PageRank this way, accurately for the top nodes after very few walks. References Levin, D. A., Peres, Y., & Wilmer, E. L. (2017). Markov Chains and Mixing Times (2nd ed.). American Mathematical Society. Lovász, L. (1993). Random walks on graphs: A survey. t: Reversed domain names and public suffixes
d: Why web graphs write google.com as com.google, and how the Public Suffix List decides where a registrable domain begins.
a: Reversed host names SURT Public Suffix List PSL Registrable domain eTLD+1
x: Common Crawl’s vertex files list com.google , com.facebook and uk.co.bbc , not google.com . Writing host names with their labels reversed is a small trick with large consequences: sorted alphabetically, reversed names keep every host of a domain, and every domain of a top-level domain, next to each other. Graph compression, range queries and prefix grouping all depend on that locality. The second half of the story is deciding where the domain part of a name ends, which takes a list, not a rule. Reversing labels A host name is a sequence of labels separated by dots, most specific first: blog.example.co.uk . Reversing the labels gives uk.co.example.blog , most general first, like a file path. Sorting reversed names produces a hierarchy: com.example com.example.blog com.example.shop com.examples uk.co.example uk.co.example.blog All of example.com ’s hosts form one contiguous run, and all .uk names come after all .com names. Sorting the forward names instead would scatter them: blog.example.com sorts among the b’s and shop.example.com among the s’s. The convention is old. Java package names ( org.apache.commons ) use it, and web archives sort their indexes by SURT, the Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , which writes http://www.example.com/a as com,example,www)/a . Common Crawl’s own URL index uses SURT keys. Why graphs care Web graph tools number nodes in sorted order. With reversed names, the numbers of related hosts sit close together: Compression. Hosts of one site link to similar targets and to each other. When related hosts get nearby numbers, successor lists repeat and the gaps between consecutive targets shrink, which is exactly what webgraph-compression exploits. Common Crawl’s vertex ids follow reversed-name order. Range queries. All domains of a top-level domain form one id range: every .de domain is a contiguous block, so “restrict to German domains” becomes a range test. Tie-breaking. Rankings with tied scores fall back on node id. Common Crawl sorts its ranks file by score with a stable sort, so ties end up in id order, which is reversed-name order (see ranks-and-scores). Public suffixes Where does the registrable domain begin? For www.example.com it is example.com , the last two labels. For www.example.co.uk it is example.co.uk , the last three, because co.uk is a suffix under which anyone can register names. No rule computes this from the name. The Public Suffix List (PSL), maintained by volunteers at Mozilla since 2007, lists such suffixes: com , co.uk , ac.jp , pvt.k12.ma.us and thousands more. The registrable domain , also called eTLD+1, is the public suffix plus one more label. The list has two sections: The ICANN section holds suffixes delegated through the domain name system: TLDs and the second-level structures registries define, such as co.uk . The private section holds suffixes that companies submit for their own platforms: github.io , blogspot.com , herokuapp.com . Browsers use these entries to stop one customer’s site from setting cookies for another’s. Whether a graph honours the private section changes its nodes. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph does not: github.io is one domain with 310,784 hosts and blogspot.com one domain with 4,113,910 hosts, though the PSL’s private section lists both as public suffixes. Each GitHub Pages site or Blogspot blog is a separate site to its owner and a separate registrable domain to a browser, but a single node in this graph. The Page, host and domain graphs entry discusses what that merging does to rankings. Names in the Common Crawl graph The 2026 domain graph spans 1,520 top-level domains and 7,482 distinct public suffixes. Its largest suffix groups: Suffix Domains .com 59,819,443 .org 6,634,711 .de 5,022,175 .net 3,751,749 .co.uk 2,691,012 Half of all domains are .com . Internationalised names appear in their ASCII-compatible xn-- form (594,228 domains), about one domain in seven contains a hyphen, and one in eight a digit. Pitfalls Matching on the last two labels is wrong for every country with second-level registries: it folds every .co.uk site into one node called co.uk . The list changes. New gTLDs and new private suffixes appear every month. A graph built with an old copy of the PSL and one built with a new copy disagree on some nodes. Hosts are not domains. A name such as www.example.com in one dataset and example.com in another are different nodes at the host level and the same node at the domain level. Normalise before joining datasets. Host counts measure DNS habits, not reach. A domain that answers for any subdomain can generate unlimited hosts, and some sites mint a subdomain per page or per user. In the 2026 graph hub.biz folds 1,222,261 hosts and adgo.kr 423,413, yet adgo.kr ranks below position 3,000,000 by harmonic centrality (see link-spam). References Mozilla Foundation. Public Suffix List. publicsuffix.org (ICANN and private sections). Internet Archive. SURT: Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , as used by the Heritrix crawler and Wayback CDX indexes. d: Groups of nodes that can all reach each other along links. They decide where a random surfer gets trapped and which nodes a spectral ranking can see.
a: SCC Strong components Condensation Tarjan's algorithm
x: Two nodes are strongly connected when each can reach the other by following links. Strong connection is an equivalence relation: every node is strongly connected to itself, the relation is symmetric by definition, and if and reach each other and and reach each other, so do and . It therefore splits the nodes into disjoint groups, the strongly connected components (SCCs). Inside a component, every node reaches every other; between components, traffic flows one way at most. The running example The running example (see The web graph ) has five SCCs: A B C D E F G The core A → B → C → A (with the shortcut A → C and the return C → A) is the only component with more than one node. D, E, F and G each form a component of their own. A, B and C reach each other, so they form one component. Every other node is a component by itself: D reaches the core but the core never reaches D; G is reached from the core but reaches nothing; E reaches everything and nothing reaches it; F only receives a link. The condensation Shrink each component to a single node and keep one arc between two components whenever some arc joins them. The result is the condensation , and it is always a directed acyclic graph: if two components could reach each other, they would be one component. For the running example: E → D → {A,B,C} → G E → {A,B,C} E → F The condensation shows the large-scale flow of a graph at a glance. Components with no incoming arcs are sources (E); components with no outgoing arcs are sinks (F, G and, at web scale, much larger groups). The The bow-tie structure picture of the web is the condensation viewed from its largest component. Why ranking cares Random surfers get trapped in sink components. A random walk that enters a component with no exits never leaves. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would drain into sinks; the damping-factor exists to pull it back out. Spectral rankings see only part of the graph. Eigenvector centrality gives zero to every node that the dominant component cannot reach. In the running example, D, E and F all get exactly zero, though D and E link into the core. Reachability bounds geometric centralities. A node’s Harmonic centrality counts only the nodes that can reach it. A node in a large component, or downstream of one, has far more candidates to count. Finding the components Two classic algorithms find all SCCs in linear time, : Tarjan’s algorithm (1972) runs one depth-first search. Each node records the order in which the search discovered it and the earliest-discovered node reachable from its subtree that is still on the stack (its low-link ). When a node’s low-link equals its own discovery index, the nodes above it on the stack form a complete component. Kosaraju’s algorithm runs two searches: one on the graph to record finishing order, then one on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order. Each tree of the second search is a component. Both are depth-first, and web graphs have paths millions of nodes long, so a recursive implementation overflows any call stack. Production code keeps an explicit stack. Common Crawl computes its components with the WebGraph framework’s StronglyConnectedComponents , which works directly on the compressed graph. Components in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph splits into 89,324,507 strongly connected components: Statistic Value Domains 119,722,885 Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) Domains outside the largest component 89,503,597 Domains with no out-links (each its own component) 76,352,306 One giant component holds a quarter of all domains. Everything else is shattered: the remaining 89.5 million domains form 89.3 million components, so nearly all of them are single domains. Every domain with no out-links is necessarily a singleton, which accounts for most of the count. A crawl-based graph understates the giant component. The crawler fetched only some of the 76 million domains with no recorded out-links; many of them do link back into the core in reality. Studies of page-level graphs find much larger giant components. Broder and colleagues found 28% of 203 million pages in theirs in 1999, and Meusel and colleagues found about half of 3.5 billion pages in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. Weak components Ignoring arc directions gives weakly connected components : groups linked by any chain of arcs, in either direction. The running example is one weak component. Web graphs typically have one weak component containing almost every node, plus many tiny islands. Weak components are cheap to find with union–find in nearly linear time, and they are the first thing to check when a graph looks wrong: a crawl that produced two large weak components probably mangled its URLs. d: The directed graph with a node for every page, host or domain and an arc for every hyperlink between them.
a: Link graph Hyperlink graph Webgraph
x: The web graph turns the web into mathematics. Each node stands for a unit of the web: a page, a host or a whole domain. Each arc stands for a hyperlink: an arc from to says that contains a link pointing at . Once the web is a graph, questions like “which site matters most?” or “how far apart are two sites?” become questions about paths and walks that an algorithm can answer. Nodes and arcs Write the graph as , with nodes and arcs. The arcs are directed : a link from to says nothing about a link back. Most link graphs also simplify the raw data in two ways: Parallel links collapse. A page that links to the same target ten times contributes one arc, not ten. At the domain level, a million links from one domain to another still make one arc. Self-loops vanish. Links from a node to itself, such as a site’s navigation menu linking to its own home page, say nothing about how the rest of the web sees it. Common Crawl’s domain graph contains no loops at all. The out-degree counts the arcs leaving and the in-degree counts the arcs arriving at . Every arc adds one to an out-degree and one to an in-degree, so both degrees average to . The Degree entry covers them in detail. A B C D E F G The running example as a web graph. Ten arcs connect seven sites. A link from E to D does not imply one from D to E. Why direction matters The two ends of a link are not equal. A site’s owner decides what the site links to , so out-links are cheap and fully under the owner’s control. Who links to a site depends on thousands of other people. That asymmetry is the reason almost every ranking method in this encyclopedia scores a node by what points at it: PageRank , Harmonic centrality , hits authorities, and plain in-degree. It is also why link-spam targets in-links. A spammer cannot easily make popular sites link to them, so they manufacture sites that do. Ignoring direction throws this information away. In an undirected version of the running example, F (linked only from E) looks exactly like a site that links only to E, though the two play opposite roles. How a crawler builds the graph Nobody holds a complete copy of the web, so every web graph is a sample built by a crawler: Fetch a page and extract every href in it. Resolve relative URLs against the page’s address and normalise them (lower-case host names, drop fragments). Map each URL to a node. A page graph keeps the full URL, a host graph keeps the host name, and a domain graph keeps the registered domain. See Page, host and domain graphs . Drop duplicates and self-loops, and add the remaining arcs. The sample is lopsided. A crawler learns the out-links of the pages it fetched, but it learns about many more pages only as link targets. Those pages enter the graph with in-links and no out-links. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, 76,352,306 of the 119,722,885 domains (63.8%) have no outgoing arcs. Most of them are sites the crawl never fetched, not sites that truly link nowhere. The dangling-nodes entry explains how ranking methods cope. More than half of all domains (56%) have in-degree 0 or 1, while 45 domains receive links from more than a million other domains each. Stored naively as pairs of 32-bit integers, those 2.45 billion arcs take 19.6 GB. The webgraph-compression entry shows how the WebGraph framework stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and still answers “who does this domain link to?” quickly. What the graph leaves out A link graph keeps only the fact that one node links to another. It drops: Where the link sits : a footer link and a link in the body of an article become identical arcs. The words of the link : see anchor-text. The link’s attributes : whether a crawler records nofollow , sponsored and ugc links depends on the pipeline. See link-attributes. Time : a graph is a snapshot. Links appear and disappear, and an expired domain can keep in-links for years after its site is gone. Each omission is a design choice, and each one changes what the rankings built on the graph mean. Commercial link indexes make different choices from Common Crawl’s, which explains some of the disagreement between their metrics (see metric-audit).
